title: Al-Mu'izz, the Giver of Honor
tomorrow: if honor is His to give, can He take it back too?
last: HE OPENS · HE KNOWS · THE TIGHTENING

lines: THE BACK OF AN ELECTRIC BILL.
cards: Thank-you speeches have a way of skipping the one person who was there before anything started. Yesterday's question: on unveiling night, who's missing from Amira's list? She notices halfway through reading it.
Dadi Fatima, who taught her to draw at the kitchen table with a pencil and the back of an electric bill, is in the kitchen, plating food for everyone, and nobody has said her name.

teach.h: IN THY HAND IS THE GOOD.
teach.b: The Qur'an teaches a prayer that says it plainly, in Pickthall's words: "Thou exaltest whom Thou wilt and Thou abasest whom Thou wilt. In Thy hand is the good."
Honor comes from His hand, not from the caption or the microphone. And surah eighty-nine, from earlier this week, adds a twist: being honored is a trial too.
The man who says "My Lord honoureth me" when things go well hears the same word as the man who says "My Lord despiseth me": nay.
Neither the honor nor the lack of it is the verdict. So what does a person do with a name that belongs to God? The same thing as with the last few: stop standing in its way.

Look at how two weeks of names sat alongside Amira's wall: a plan, a making, a form; a door that closed and one that opened; a worry known before it was told; a squeeze and a widening; a caption where pride stepped down and someone quiet went up.
And the name for honor points at a kitchen. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in the Qur'an, honor is a trial as much as a gift.

how: Muslims recite the prayer of Qur'an 3:26, which names the One who exalts and abases, and the tradition honors elders and those who serve quietly as part of good character.

o: the One who repays every insult received
the One who gives honor to whom He wills
the One who praises people for their fame

games.q: two weeks of names — tap the pairs.
p: he opens, sometimes through a no

s: being honored by people is proof that Allah is pleased with you
surah eighty-nine calls honor a trial too, and answers 'my Lord honoureth me' with nay.
the Qur'an's prayer in surah three says the good is in His hand
Thou exaltest whom Thou wilt and Thou abasest whom Thou wilt. In Thy hand is the good.

games.q: review round: a friend's worried that a tight month means she's out of favor with God. which line from the last two weeks fits?
o: the tightening: a trial, not a verdict.
he lowers: the proud get brought down.
he knows: even the leaf nobody saw.
games.why: al-Qabid tightens as a trial, and the Qur'an answers 'my Lord despiseth me' with nay. the others are true, but they answer different worries.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write by hand the name of one person who gets overlooked: a grandparent, a teacher from years back, someone who cleans where you work. Under it, write one thing they gave you.
Keep your hand on the paper for the rest of the sit, and let their name be said, at least here.

wordCard.voice: Al-Mu'izz: the Giver of Honor, in whose hand is the good, and whose honor can find someone plating food in a back kitchen.

orig.note: Arabic: the Giver of Honor, the One who strengthens and honors. beside al-Mudhill in the traditional list.

carryVoice: The line to keep: honor is his to give, and he sees the kitchen too. Two weeks, one wall, done.
